analysis.one_liner: Moves large interstate class-action lawsuits from state courts into federal court.
analysis.headline: The Senate fell one vote short of the 60 needed to even debate the bill — 59 to 39 on the procedural vote — and it died without ever getting an up-or-down vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let defendants move most large interstate class-action lawsuits — claims over $5 million where plaintiffs and defendants live in different states — out of state courts and into federal court, and make it much easier for any defendant to force that move. It also includes rules aimed at abuses of class actions, such as settlements that give class members coupons while lawyers collect big fees, and requirements that settlement notices be written in plain language. The jurisdictional change is the core of the bill; the consumer protections are narrow additions.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies facing consumer, employment, or product class actions. Federal courts are a friendlier forum for defendants: they are harder on class certification, apply state consumer-protection law less expansively, and settlement amounts tend to be smaller. The bill also lets a single defendant move a case to federal court without every defendant's consent, and lets a plaintiff class member force removal — a provision that could dislodge cases plaintiffs deliberately filed in their home state court.

how_it_helps.text: Grants federal courts jurisdiction over class actions exceeding $5 million whenever any plaintiff class member and any defendant are citizens of different states, so interstate class actions would no longer stay in state court.

Lets any single defendant remove a class action to federal court without the consent of all defendants, and makes orders sending a class action back to state court appealable — reversing the usual rule that such orders cannot be appealed.

Bars court approval of settlements where class members would receive coupons or non-cash benefits unless the judge holds a hearing and finds the settlement fair, and bars settlements that leave some class members with a net loss after paying class counsel.
Requires settlement notices to class members to include a plain-language summary of rights, obligations, and the dollar amount of attorney fees being sought.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, employees, and small investors with claims against large companies. Their class actions would move to federal court, where certification of a class is harder and the state-law remedies they are suing under are applied more cautiously — the practical effect is fewer certified classes and smaller recoveries. Plaintiff-side class action firms would bear the direct loss of the state-court forum.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers and workers suing large companies

drawbacks.text: The coupon-settlement provisions respond to a real abuse: some settlements have awarded class members coupons of little value while class counsel collected millions in fees, and some notices were so confusing that members could not exercise their rights to opt out.

The bill's findings argue that some state courts act with bias against out-of-state defendants and impose one state's legal views on residents of other states, which supporters cited as a reason for a neutral federal forum.

The honest cost of those protections: they ride along with the jurisdictional shift, which is the provision companies and consumer groups alike recognized as the bill's main event. Moving cases to federal court makes it harder to certify classes under state consumer-protection laws, which is precisely why defendant industries backed the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections in the bill are genuine but small compared with what the jurisdictional change does. Shifting nearly every large interstate class action into federal court primarily changes outcomes for the companies being sued — fewer certified classes, smaller settlements — and only secondarily for class members. A bill written purely to fix coupon-settlement abuses did not need to rewrite federal jurisdiction to do it; bundling the two means the main effect would have fallen on ordinary plaintiffs' ability to bring claims at all.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate took a procedural vote to open debate on the bill, and it failed 59-39 — one vote short of the 60 needed — so the bill never got a real floor vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on October 16, 2003, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors, and it was placed on the Senate calendar the next day without going through committee.
Supporters moved for cloture — a vote to end debate and proceed to the bill — just four days after introduction, signaling they wanted a quick floor vote before opponents could organize.
On October 22, 2003, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 59-39. Under Senate rules it needed 60 votes; every Republican present but one voted yes, and only 8 of 48 Democrats joined them.
The bill never received an up-or-down vote on its merits and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers with pending claims and the plaintiff-side class action bar kept the state-court forum that corporate defendants had spent years trying to close off; companies that would have faced federal class actions got no change in the law.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, with a group of original cosponsors, got it placed directly on the Senate calendar, then moved cloture within days to force it to the floor.

for.name: 3 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the bipartisan cover its backers needed to try for an early floor vote.

for.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business coalitions
for.role: Industry lobby groups for corporate defendants
for.what_they_did: Ran a sustained campaign for federal class-action jurisdiction, making it one of the business lobby's top priorities of the decade.

against.name: 38 of 48 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on cloture on the motion to proceed, denying the 60 votes needed to bring the bill to the floor.

against.name: Consumer and civil justice groups and plaintiff trial lawyers
against.role: Opposition coalition (consumer advocacy organizations, trial lawyer associations)
against.what_they_did: Argued the bill would shut consumer and employment class actions out of state courts where those claims are strongest, and lobbied senators to block it.

sides.party_line_note: On the 59-39 cloture vote, 50 of 51 Republicans voted yes while only 8 of 48 Democrats did — the bill had bipartisan cosponsors but opposition was overwhelmingly Democratic.

industries.industry: Corporate defendants in class actions (insurers, banks, consumer product and drug companies)
industries.note: The bill would give them the right to move large class actions into federal court, where class certification is harder and state-law remedies are applied more narrowly — shrinking their exposure to consumer, employment, and product liability claims. Its benefit to ordinary people is limited to the coupon-settlement and notice rules.

The bill removes the state-court forum where most consumer and employment class actions are filed and certified, directly cutting the business of firms that prosecute those cases. That same forum is what gives ordinary plaintiffs leverage over large defendants.

industries.industry: State-court systems and state attorneys general
industries.note: Large class actions would be pulled out of state courts, removing cases that enforce state consumer-protection laws and reducing state courts' role as a check on national companies. The bill's notice provisions would give state officials notice of settlements but no new enforcement power.
